e.etymology: A surname used as a first name. As an Irish surname Hoy is a shortened English form of O hEochaidh, descendant of Eochaidh.
A spelling of Sammie, a pet form of Samuel that was also given to girls in the South around 1900. Samuel is from Hebrew Shemuel, read as name of God or God has heard.

e.meaning: first son or harmonious man (varies with the kanji)
e.etymology: A Japanese men's name whose sense depends on the characters: kazu is most often written as one or first, or as harmony, and o as man, husband or hero.
namesakes: Kazuo Ishiguro (Nobel-winning novelist, The Remains of the Day)

e.etymology: A respelling of Jeremy, the medieval English form of Jeremiah, from Hebrew Yirmeyahu, the Lord will exalt.
The Swedish spelling of Gustav, from Old Swedish Gotstaf, usually read as Old Norse Gautr (the Geats) plus stafr (staff). It is the name of six Swedish kings.
The Finnish form of Reynold and German Reinhold, from Germanic ragin (counsel) and wald (rule). In the US it was a Finnish American name of the early 1900s.
The French form of Aurora, the Latin word for dawn and the name of the Roman goddess of the dawn.
Possibly an English form of the Irish name Eithne. It is also the name of Mount Etna, the Sicilian volcano, and of several American towns.

assoc.t: Mount Etna, the active volcano in Sicily

e.etymology: As a first name it belongs with Cordero and Cordarius, American boys' names of the 1980s built on the Cord- opening. Cordaro is also an Italian surname.
An English surname meaning son of Hob, a medieval pet form of Robert. Its 1898 peak honored Richmond P. Hobson, a naval hero of the Spanish-American War.
A short form of Patricia and Patrick, both from Latin patricius, a patrician or member of the Roman nobility.
A short form of Pamela, a name Sir Philip Sidney invented for his romance Arcadia around 1590, apparently from Greek pan (all) and meli (honey).
namesakes: Pam Grier (actress, Foxy Brown and Jackie Brown)

assoc.t: Pam Beesly, the receptionist on The Office

e.etymology: A medieval rhyming nickname for Richard, by way of Rick. Richard joins the Germanic elements ric (ruler, power) and hard (strong, brave).

assoc.t: vulgar slang for penis, and for an obnoxious man

e.note: Now mainly heard as vulgar slang for penis and as an insult; the name has all but vanished.

e.etymology: A pet form of Ann and Nancy, given as a full name in the 1800s. Ann comes from the Hebrew name Hannah, grace or favor.
e.note: Sounds the same as nanny, a word for a child's caregiver, a grandmother and a female goat.

e.etymology: A respelling of Betty, a pet form of Elizabeth, from Hebrew Elisheva, my God is an oath.
The English adjective gay in its older sense of merry and carefree, from Old French gai. It was a girls' name in the first half of the 1900s.
e.note: Gay now chiefly means homosexual, and the name dropped out of use as that sense took over.

e.etymology: Usually taken as a short form of Aletha, a variant of Alethea, from Greek aletheia, truth.
A spelling of Sandra, the short form of Alessandra and Alexandra, from Greek alexein (to defend) and aner (man).
A spelling of Sharon, the Hebrew name of the fertile coastal plain of Israel, praised in the Song of Songs for its flowers. It became a given name in the 20th century.
An American name of the early 1900s that joins the La- prefix to the ending of Yvonne.
A feminine form of Earl made with the -ine ending. Earl is the English title of nobility, from Old English eorl, nobleman or warrior.
A spelling of Ernestine shaped by the English word earnest. Ernestine is the French feminine form of Ernest, from the Germanic word ernust, serious.
A spelling of Kathy, the pet form of Katherine and Kathleen, from Greek Aikaterine. The traditional meaning pure comes from a later link with Greek katharos.
namesakes: Kathie Lee Gifford (TV host and singer)

e.etymology: A pet form of Augusta, and for boys of Gus, Augustus and Gustave. Augusta comes from Latin augustus, venerable or majestic.
A feminine form of Earl made with the -ene ending. Earl is the English title of nobility, from Old English eorl, nobleman or warrior.
A spelling of Megan, the Welsh pet form of Margaret, from Greek margarites, pearl. The -agh- gives a Welsh name an Irish look.
A spelling of Tammy, the pet form of Tamara, from Hebrew tamar, date palm. Tammy took off after the 1957 film Tammy and the Bachelor and its hit song.
namesakes: Tammi Terrell (Motown singer and Marvin Gaye's duet partner)

e.etymology: A contracted form of Tamara, the Russian form of the biblical Tamar, from Hebrew tamar, date palm.
namesakes: Tamra Judge (The Real Housewives of Orange County)

e.etymology: An old English pet form of Margaret, from Greek margarites, pearl.
namesakes: Madge (the manicurist in Palmolive's long-running TV ads)

e.etymology: A respelling of Crystal made popular by Krystle Carrington, Linda Evans's character on the 1980s soap Dynasty. The word comes from Greek krystallos, ice or rock crystal.

assoc.t: Krystle Carrington, heroine of the soap Dynasty

e.etymology: A spelling of Tamika, an African-American name of the 1970s. Tamika is often traced to the Japanese name Tamiko, heard in the 1962 film A Girl Named Tamiko.
